intro: The piano begins alone with tolling chords, then gives the first melody to the orchestra. Listen for the changing division of labour: the soloist supplies accompaniment, sings, and turns the same material into a march.
question: When is the soloist the singer, and when the accompaniment?

sections.label: Climax and return
sections.mNote: orchestral first subject returns against march-like piano writing

sections.label: Second subject · quieter restatement
sections.mNote: second subject moves to solo horn in A♭ major

relations.label: The first-subject music returns
relations.basis: The first subject and its associated material return in the recapitulation with changed piano writing. The excerpts lie in the later part of the opening subject group and its returning continuation, rather than at the large climax itself. CENS diagonal mean 0.931, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 369.5 s (cache/form/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-moderato.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Chords before the tune
cues.text: The concerto opens with repeated piano chords before its first extended melody. Listen for the growing weight of these widely spaced attacks and the low note beneath them, rather than expecting a tune immediately.
cues.evidence: The solo chordal introduction is in the score. Relative level rises steadily across roughly 0:00–0:20, before a strong measured change around 0:24.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody and moving accompaniment
cues.text: In the first-subject passage, the orchestra carries the melody while the piano supplies running broken chords. Keep the layers separate: the part with the most notes is not necessarily the part carrying the tune.
cues.evidence: The score assigns these roles in the first subject. A strong change around 0:24 and a sustained C-centred span after it support the approximate placement; individual entrances are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After the First Symphony
cues.text: The failure of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897 damaged his confidence as a composer. The Second Concerto followed a period of difficulty in completing new work, not an uninterrupted sequence of public successes.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony account documents the 1897 failure and subsequent difficulty composing: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Melody versus activity
cues.text: Throughout the opening section, distinguish the bass, the running figures and the slower melodic line. Accompaniment can be technically demanding without becoming the principal melody.
cues.evidence: This is a score-based listening strategy for the first-subject texture, not a claim of a new entrance at 1:41.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The doctor in the dedication
cues.text: From January to April 1900, Rachmaninoff consulted Nikolai Dahl, a physician who used hypnosis and repeated encouragement. Dahl was also an amateur musician. The concerto’s dedication names him; it does not establish which part of the treatment helped most.
cues.evidence: Mandel documents the treatment and dedication while noting uncertainty about the components of the “cure”: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: A more lyrical second subject
cues.text: The second-subject span gives the piano a sustained melodic role in E♭ major. Compare that role with the opening’s moving accompaniment: the soloist can change its function without leaving the foreground.
cues.evidence: The score gives the second subject to the piano. A quiet reset around 2:25 and E♭-centred writing around 2:40–2:45 support this passage estimate, not a precise solo entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The phrase expands
cues.text: Through the second-subject expansion, follow the longer melodic notes beneath the smaller figures. A phrase can gather weight without requiring every attack to carry equal emphasis.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises across roughly 3:00–3:25, with increased activity later in the span. The report supports the broad contour rather than a detailed account of the pianist’s phrasing.

cues.title: Themes in smaller pieces
cues.text: In the development, fragments of the earlier subjects travel beyond their original settings. Listen for recurring rhythms and contours rather than waiting only for complete tunes in familiar keys.
cues.evidence: The score’s development follows the exposition. A quieter passage after about 4:00 and further changes through 5:08 support this approximate placement; the report does not recognise the themes itself.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Moscow, November 1901
cues.text: Rachmaninoff played the complete concerto’s premiere in Moscow on 9 November 1901, with Alexander Siloti conducting. Siloti was his cousin and former piano teacher. The first movement was completed after the other two had already been performed.
cues.evidence: Mandel’s Boston Symphony note documents the premiere, Siloti’s relationship to Rachmaninoff and the order of completion: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Sustained and moving layers
cues.text: During the middle span, listen for the contrast between sustained sound and more closely spaced attacks. These different rates of movement can prepare a build before its largest swell arrives.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks are sparse around 5:05–5:20 and increase around 5:25–5:40. The report cannot assign those attacks to particular instruments.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Building towards the return
cues.text: The later development gathers weight across several phrases. Keep earlier melodic fragments in mind as the texture becomes denser; the coming return will place familiar material in a more forceful setting.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 5:45–6:20. The score places the climactic return after this build, but the first returning note has not been aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The return, made martial
cues.text: At the climactic return, the first subject is set against march-like piano writing. Compare the renewed theme with its first appearance: the accompanying activity has changed the balance of the passage.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the march-like recapitulation. The recording’s sustained highest-level span around 6:20–7:00 suggests its placement, without identifying an exact thematic entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The crest falls away
cues.text: The sustained crest gives way to a substantial withdrawal. Compare how quickly the recorded weight recedes with the longer build that prepared it.
cues.evidence: The report shows a marked fall in relative level around 7:00–7:10, after the prolonged higher-level span. It does not identify particular instruments withdrawing.

cues.title: A quieter melodic return
cues.text: In the later, quieter restatement of the lyrical material, compare the melody’s function with its earlier appearance. A familiar theme can return with a different balance between foreground and accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The score includes a quieter second-subject restatement. The sustained low-activity span around 8:20–8:45 supports an approximate placement, but cannot identify a horn solo by itself.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Listen towards the ending
cues.text: Through the quieter late passage, listen for how phrases prepare an ending rather than another full contrast. The first movement ultimately closes in C minor; the concerto’s major-key conclusion belongs to its finale.
cues.evidence: The movement’s final minor key and the concerto’s final major key come from the score. Passing key estimates around 9:40–9:55 are not treated as individual chord identifications.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The ending holds back
cues.text: The closing section spends time reducing the music before its final concentrated burst. Listen for the continued movement within the quieter phrases rather than expecting an immediate emphatic ending.
cues.evidence: The score’s closing span follows the later returns. The report shows comparatively low level around 10:00–10:35 before the final build.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The final increase
cues.text: The closing passage gathers attacks and weight before the C-minor ending. Listen beyond the final chords to their short decay.
cues.evidence: The report shows increasing attacks and relative level around 10:40–10:55, then a sharp fall through 11:05. C minor is the score’s destination; no exact final chord time is claimed.

transitions.title: The bell strokes become flowing accompaniment
transitions.how: The piano’s tolling chords grow above a recurring low F, building pressure before C minor becomes the first theme’s home. The bass moves to C and the piano breaks its vertical chords into running arpeggios; strings and clarinet now supply the long melody. This is a transfer of function as well as an orchestral entrance. The soloist’s earlier isolated attacks become a continuous moving layer beneath somebody else’s song, while the weight accumulated in the introduction supports the new phrase.
transitions.evidence: The first-subject boundary is 0:24, a strong measured change after the introduction’s rising level. F-centred opening windows give way to C-centred sound. The score supplies the low-F bell introduction, C-minor arrival and division between orchestral melody and piano arpeggios; the report does not identify the individual instruments.

transitions.title: The soloist changes from movement to song
transitions.how: The faster piano transition and its emphatic cadential gestures prepare E♭ major, the relative major of C minor. B♭ dominant harmony now points towards E♭ rather than another C-minor arrival. After the accumulated motion, the texture withdraws and the soloist takes the second subject as a sustained upper melody, lightly supported by the orchestra. The same keyboard that supplied the first subject’s restless accompaniment becomes the singer; the longer note values make the change audible before the whole tune has unfolded.
transitions.evidence: The second-subject marker is 2:30. Analysis shows the quiet reset around 2:25 and E♭-centred writing around 2:40–2:45. The score supplies the più mosso transition, cadential preparation and E♭-major piano subject. The marker locates the passage, not a verified first melodic note or dominant resolution.

transitions.title: The closing rush breaks into thematic fragments
transitions.how: The exposition’s E♭-major closing activity subsides, and fragments of the two subjects replace their complete statements. The piano’s figurations and orchestral answers can now be sequenced against changing bass notes rather than held within one lyrical paragraph. E♭ major ceases to be the destination; minor-key colouring and shifting harmonic supports loosen the ground. Rachmaninoff preserves recognisable rhythms and contours while changing their size and instrumental owners, making the development a continuation made from smaller pieces.
transitions.evidence: The development boundary is 4:00. The level report shows a sharp withdrawal there, with further changes through 5:08. The score supplies the agitated exposition close and subsequent fragmentation of both subjects. The provisional relation study does not align the development, and passing key estimates are not treated as identified pivot chords.

transitions.title: The build becomes the returning theme’s accompaniment
transitions.how: The development’s repeated figures, acceleration and rising weight prepare a C-minor return without a clearing of the texture. When the orchestra restores the first subject, the piano does not resume its original arpeggios: it presses a march-like idea against the broad tune. The bass and full orchestral sonority establish the home key while the soloist retains the development’s rhythmic pressure. Arrival and climax coincide, so recognition comes through the melody within the crowded sound rather than through a fresh quiet opening.
transitions.evidence: The climax-and-return marker is 6:20. Analysis shows a sustained build from about 5:45 and the highest-level span around 6:20–7:00. The score supplies the C-minor, march-like recapitulation. A provisional relation supports later first-subject material around 7:28–7:42, not the exact initial return at this marker.

transitions.title: A chromatic descent leaves the horn alone
transitions.how: The piano’s continuation of the first subject contracts into a descending chromatic passage and a very quiet A♭-major chord. The lyrical second subject then passes to a solo horn. Its exposition key, E♭ major, has been replaced by A♭ major, the submediant region of C minor, and its earlier piano voice by a sustained orchestral one. The bass settles while the surrounding activity falls away: a change of key, owner and density makes the returning melody sound newly exposed.
transitions.evidence: The quieter-restatement boundary is 8:20. Analysis shows very low activity across 8:20–8:45 and A♭-major estimates around 8:25–8:40. The score supplies the descending chromatic piano passage, quiet A♭ chord and horn restatement; the feature report cannot identify that soloist or time its first note.

transitions.title: The major colouring yields to the minor close
transitions.how: The late piano arpeggios briefly offer C-major colouring, but the closing section restores E♭ and the movement’s C minor. Marked Meno mosso, it holds back rather than immediately repeating the earlier climax. Material from the first subject is reduced and gathered over a more deliberate bass before the final acceleration and forceful G-to-C cadences. The closing seam therefore works by delaying the expected burst: the home key returns before its final weight does.
transitions.evidence: The closing-section boundary is 9:56, a strong measured change. The report places a quiet span around 10:00–10:35 before the final build. The score supplies the preceding C-major arpeggios, Meno mosso first-subject coda and ultimate C-minor authentic cadences. Passing chroma estimates alone do not establish the modal change.

timeline.note: Piano alone: widely spaced bell chords build above the recurring low F.
Clarinets and upper strings sing the first subject; piano arpeggios flow above pizzicato cellos and basses.
The string melody broadens as woodwinds and horns fill the harmony around the piano’s running accompaniment.
Piano figures come forward; sustained flute and clarinet chords give way to horn and string punctuation.
The piano takes the lyrical second subject; quiet strings and reed responses leave its melody exposed.
Woodwinds answer the piano as the lyrical paragraph expands towards brass-supported closing gestures.
Piano fragments and woodwind replies replace complete themes; muted strings sustain and punctuate the changing harmony.
Flutes and oboes carry longer notes against piano figures; horns and lower strings prepare the build.
Brass calls, sustained winds and rising string weight gather around the piano’s increasingly chordal rhythm.
The orchestra restores the first subject while the piano presses its march-like counterline through the tutti.
The piano takes the continuing theme; heavy brass withdraws and woodwinds answer over quieter strings.
Solo horn sings the second subject in A♭ major over repeated string chords; the piano initially rests.
The piano resumes the foreground; soft wind chords and string lines surround its late arpeggios.
Muted strings reduce the first subject over deliberate piano figures; bassoon and horn support the quieter coda.
Full winds, brass and timpani reinforce the piano and strings in the final C-minor drive.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
